newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico peso ends down on speculation and panic.
newsitem.headline: Mexico peso ends down on speculation and panic.

text.p: The Mexican peso clawed back some lost ground when dealers dumped surplus dollars in late trade but still closed substantially weaker on Wednesday, after it was mauled by speculation and panic during the session, traders said.
The benchmark 48-hour peso and its 24-hour stablemate closed six and 6.2 centavos weaker, respectively, at 7.8400/7.8500 and 7.8350/7.8450 per dollar.
The same-day peso closed earlier 8.9 centavos weaker at 7.8300/7.8400 per dollar.
The peso was battered in early trade when dollars flowed out of Mexico as foreign dealers decided that Tuesday night's primary rate hikes were insufficient to offset the risk of investing in Mexico.
"Foreign investors said that rate hikes were not enough to keep them here. Now we have to wait for inflation figures tomorrow," said a dealer.
Consumer inflation data for the first half of October were expected on Thursday afternoon. Analysts were expecting figures of around 0.65 percent.

Traders said the speculative onslaught against the peso was also unleashed by comments in the local press by U.S. economics professor Rudiger Dornbusch, which said that the peso needed to be devalued by another 20 percent, to about nine per dollar.

Dornbusch has been a frequent and leading critic of Mexican official policy towards the peso. Traders said his comments tended to recall the sudden and unexpected devaluation of December 1994, which plunged the Mexican economy into a recession from which it has yet to recover.
"Dornbusch's comments are really shaking the market," a trader said.
Dornbusch did, however, say at a conference held at Banco Santander's New York headquarters on Wednesday that a sudden devaluation was unnecessary.

"...a maxi-devaluation in Mexico would be totally inappropriate. The peso should, though, start depreciating at the pace of inflation to maintain the existing level of competitiveness," a Santander news release quoted Dornbusch as saying.
"...by the end of the year, P$8/US$ (eight pesos per dollar) would be the rate realistically emerging from such a strategy," Dornbusch added.
Traders said that unconfirmed reports of Dornbusch's comments also helped to prevent the peso sliding further.
